quarantineReason: Per pipeline rule, a README license statement alone (with no LICENSE file and no SPDX declaration anywhere in the tree) is verdict quarantine, not vendor or reject. Exact wording found at README.md, 'License' section: "Skills are free to use and distribute. API access for enriched output requires a paid plan." This is a plain-English permission statement, not a license grant with defined terms (no copyright line, no warranty disclaimer, no explicit redistribution/modification/sublicensing rights, no named license such as MIT/Apache/BSD) -- it cannot be treated as a verifiable redistributable license. Content quality and relevance were otherwise strong enough that most of these 5 skills would clear the vendor bar on rubric total alone. Action to unblock: ask the author to add a real LICENSE file (or an SPDX declaration) confirming and formalizing the stated 'free to use and distribute' intent; on a pinned commit that adds one, re-evaluate normally.

skillsEnumerated.assessment: Read SKILL.md in full (330 lines). Audits AI-powered interfaces (chat, copilot, agentic workflows, voice, AI-enhanced forms/search) against a named 44-principle taxonomy (uxuiprinciples 'Part V: AI and Specialized Domains'), with a 7-type interface classifier, per-type principle-selection tables, an AI-specific severity model with an explicit auto-critical escalation rule for irreversible-action violations, and a strict JSON output contract with worked examples. This is the task's named flagship candidate for this repo and the strongest of the 5 -- a genuinely distinct AI-interface-specific evaluation method not covered by the registry's general design-critique cluster or by agentic-ui-review. Conformance is only 1: frontmatter carries non-spec `version`, `author`, `homepage`, `tags`, and an `env.UXUI_API_KEY` block, and the skill body opens with a `toolbox` TOML block wiring two `curl` calls (with `Authorization: Bearer ${UXUI_API_KEY}`) to `uxuiprinciples.com/api/v1/principles` -- an undeclared third-party paid API. This is optional/degradable (the skill explicitly runs on internal LLM knowledge and sets `api_enriched: false` when the key is absent or calls fail), so it is not a security disqualifier, but it is a real host/vendor coupling worth a curator's attention if this is ever unblocked and vendored -- likely worth stripping the toolbox block or making the API-dependence more clearly optional in the SKILL.md prose itself, not only in fallback logic.

Read SKILL.md in full (261 lines). Evaluates interface descriptions against a 168-principle, 6-part taxonomy (Cognitive Foundations, Visual Design, Interaction Design, Information Architecture, AI/Emerging Interfaces, Human-Centered Design) with named principle codes (e.g. F.1.1.02), a per-interface-type part-selection table, a 0-100 scoring/banding formula, and a strict JSON output contract with worked examples. Same toolbox/API-key coupling pattern as ai-interface-reviewer (curl calls to uxuiprinciples.com). Overlaps the registry's existing design-review/interface-review/better-interface cluster on general ground, but the codified 168-principle taxonomy with stable citation codes is a meaningfully different, more citation-oriented method -- would likely be a strong vendor candidate if licensed.

Read SKILL.md in full (333 lines). Detects 8 named UX 'smells' (antipatterns) across 6 categories (efficiency, error-prevention, feedback, learnability, accessibility, consistency) with symptom-matching rules, severity guidelines per smell, and remediation recipes. Same toolbox/API-key pattern. A distinct smell-taxonomy framing versus the registry's existing heuristic/critique skills, though the named smell set (8 items) is narrower than uxui-evaluator's.

Read SKILL.md in full (281 lines). Runs preflight (before-design) and postflight (before-ship) checklists for 5 named flow types (onboarding, forms, pricing, dashboard, empty-states), each with a metric target and gated ship-readiness logic. README marks this skill 'API Required (pro)' -- unlike the other 4, it is NOT meaningfully usable without a paid `UXUI_API_KEY` for its core flow-checklist data (the skill body says the internal-knowledge fallback 'lacks live smell linkage and severity metadata'). This pushes conformance to 0 under the rubric's 'hard-wired private services' criterion even setting the license question aside -- this one skill would likely be reject or not-vendored-keeper even if the repo were licensed, unlike its 4 siblings.

Read SKILL.md in full (331 lines). Pre-generation context injection for AI coding tools: maps 16 component types (forms, tables, dashboards, checkout, ai-chat, etc.) to relevant UX principles and assembles a paste-ready system-context block with UX guardrails baked in, before a developer generates a component. Same toolbox/API-key pattern. This is coding-assistant tooling rather than a review/audit skill -- relevance 2 (clear design application, materially about generation not evaluation) rather than 3.

securityNotes: All 5 SKILL.md files read in full at the pinned commit (via a local codeload tarball extraction of the tiny 24KB repo). Prose-plus-TOML-toolbox skills only -- no scripts, no binaries. Every one of the 5 skills embeds a `toolbox` TOML block with 1-3 `curl` tool definitions calling `https://uxuiprinciples.com/api/v1/...` endpoints with `Authorization: Bearer ${UXUI_API_KEY}` when the (optional, user-supplied) API key is set; this is a declared, documented, degradable integration with the skill author's own commercial API (not a hidden or undeclared credential-exfiltration path -- the env var is named and described in frontmatter, and every skill runs correctly without it) but is exactly the kind of 'undeclared private service' the rubric flags for a curator's attention, and is noted per-skill above. No hidden instructions, no exfiltration beyond the documented optional API calls, no instruction to bypass user rules, no download-and-execute.
